documentNotes.title: General instructions
documentNotes.statement:
1. There are 2 questions, each worth 25 points. You have **80** minutes to solve them, of which :

   (a) **20** minutes for reading the question and preparing for the observations,

   (b) **40** minutes to perform all the observations in the planetarium (20 minutes for each questions),

   (c) **20** minutes for calculations and finishing your work.

2. Additional time is allowed to move to and from the planetarium.

3. Along with the questions you will be given a map of the sky, for use with both questions. The map is for epoch J 2000.0, using a polar projection with a linear scale in declination, and covers stars down to about $5^{\mathrm{th}}$ magnitude. You will also be given paper for working and notes, writing implements, a pencil sharpener and an eraser.

   Please take everything from the desk in the first room with you to the planetarium dome, as you will be going to a different room afterwards to finish your work.

4. At your place in the dome you will find a torch and clipboard. Please leave these two items behind for the next contestant.

5. Only answers given in the appropriate places on the question sheet and on the map of the sky will be assessed. The additional worksheets will not be assessed.

6. Clearly mark every page with your code number.

documentNotes.title: About the questions
documentNotes.statement: **Note:** Azimuth is counted from $0^{\circ}$ to $360^{\circ}$ starting at S through W, N, E.

problems.title: Earth
problems.statement:
In Question 1 :

1. The sky is stationary, the observer is on the surface of the Earth.

2. Visible on the sky are: a comet, the Moon and a nova of about $2^{\mathrm{nd}}$ magnitude.

3. From the $11^{\mathrm{th}}$ minute, a grid representing horizontal coordinates will be projected on the sky, and will remain on until the end of the question.

parts.label: A)
parts.statement: On the map of the sky, mark (with a cross) and label the nova (mark it “N”) and the Moon (mark it with a Moon symbol) and draw the shape and position of the comet.

parts.label: B)
parts.statement:
In the table below, circle only those objects which are above the astronomical horizon.

Note: you will lose 1 point for every incorrect answer.

| M20 – Triffid Nebula | o Cet – Mira | δ CMa – Wezen |
|---|---|---|
| α Cyg – Deneb | M57 – Ring Nebula | β Per – Algol |
| δ Cep – Alrediph | α Boo – Arcturus | M44 – Praesepe (Beehive Cluster) |

parts.label: C)
parts.statement: When the coordinate grid is visible, mark on the map the northern part of the local meridian (from the zenith to the horizon) and the ecliptic north pole (with a cross and marked “P”).

parts.label: D)
parts.statement:
For the displayed sky, give the :

geographical latitude of the observer : $\varphi = \dots\dots\dots$ ,

Local Sidereal Time : $\theta = \dots\dots\dots$ ,

time of year, by circling the calendar month :

Jan, Feb, Mar, Apr, May, Jun, Jul, Aug, Sep, Oct, Nov, Dec.

parts.label: E)
parts.statement:
Give the names of the objects, whose approximate horizontal coordinates are :

azimuth $A_1 = 45^{\circ}$ and altitude $h_1 = 58^{\circ}$ : $\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots$ ,

azimuth $A_2 = 278^{\circ}$ and altitude $h_2 = 20^{\circ}$ : $\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots$ .

(If you can, use Bayer designations, IAU abbreviations and Messier numbers or English or Latin names.)

parts.label: F)
parts.statement:
Give the horizontal coordinates (azimuth, altitude) of :

Sirius ($\alpha$ CMa) : $A_3 = \dots\dots\dots$ ; $h_3 = \dots\dots\dots$

The Andromeda Galaxy (M 31) : $A_4 = \dots\dots\dots$ ; $h_4 = \dots\dots\dots$

parts.label: G)
parts.statement:
Give the equatorial coordinates of the star marked on the sky with a red arrow :

$\alpha = \dots\dots\dots\dots$ ; $\delta = \dots\dots\dots\dots$

problems.title: Mars
problems.statement:
In Question 2 :

1. Four consecutive days on the surface of Mars will be shown.

2. There is a Martian base visible on the horizon.

3. During the Martian daytime the sky will be slightly brightened.

4. The moons of Mars and the other planets will not be displayed.

5. The local meridian will be continuously visible on the sky.

figures.alt: Two identical blank circles for sketches, each with a horizontal diameter marked S on the left and N on the right, a dot at the centre, the label Zenith at the top and Nadir at the bottom.
A horizontal time axis with an arrow labelled t, divided by tick marks into four equal intervals labelled spring, summer, autumn and winter.

parts.label: H)
parts.statement: Give the areographic (Martian) latitude of the observer : $\varphi = \dots\dots\dots$

parts.label: I)
parts.statement:
Give the altitudes of upper ($h_u$) and lower ($h_l$) culmination of :

Pollux (β Gem) : $h_u = \dots\dots\dots$ ; $h_l = \dots\dots\dots$ ,

Deneb (α Cyg) $h_u = \dots\dots\dots$ ; $h_l = \dots\dots\dots$ ,

parts.label: J)
parts.statement:
Give the areocentric (Martian) declination of :

Regulus (α Leo) $\delta = \dots\dots\dots$ .

Toliman (α Cen) $\delta = \dots\dots\dots$ .

parts.label: K)
parts.statement: Sketch diagrams to illustrate your working in questions (I) and (J) above :

parts.label: L)
parts.statement: on the map of the sky, mark (with a cross) and label (“M”) the Martian celestial North Pole.

parts.label: M)
parts.statement:
Give the azimuth of the observer as seen from the Martian base :

$A = \dots\dots\dots$ .

parts.label: N)
parts.statement:
Estimate the location of the base on Mars, and circle the appropriate description :

*a.* near the Equator

*b.* near the northern Tropic circle

*c.* near the northern Arctic circle

*d.* near the North Pole

parts.label: O)
parts.statement: The time axis below shows the Martian year and the seasons in the northern hemisphere. Mark the date represented by the planetarium display on the axis.
